docs.title: Joanne Kyger, Eleni Sikelianos, Akila Oliver, and Anne Waldman, panel, Cultural activism and writing, June, 2003.

docs.creator: Brown, Lee Ann; Jarnot, Lisa; Mayer, Bernadette
docs.description: First half of a reading with Lisa Jarnot, Lee Ann Brown and Bernadette Mayer. Jarnot reads "Ode," "Hockey night in Canada," "Poem," "On the lawn chair," "O life force," "From Carlyle," "Suddenly last summer," "Lake of fire," "Brooklyn anchorage," "Past noon," "Poem beginning with a line from Frank Lima," "The song between: After Philip Lamentia." Brown sings Helen Adam's "I love my love" and reads "The car return trip," "August Valentine," "Aylene," "Present beau: Robin Blaser," "Shady grove," "Poetry, music, nature," "Dear rod moth," "Erasers," "Murals," "Animal planet," "Villanelle on being alone," "Sustain petal" and "Oba agnus infloresence." Mayer reads "To a politician," "Landlord," "My father was a horse's ass," about ten minutes of epigrams, "On sleep" and "Mind of hour." (Continues on 99P015)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Lisa Jarnot, Lee Ann Brown and Bernadette Mayer reading, June, 1999.

docs.creator: Myles, Eileen; Ondaatje, Michael
docs.description: Second half of a poetry reading at the Fox Theater, featuring Michael Ondaatje reading from The English Patient and other works, and Eileen Myles reading "Robin" from Chelsea Girls. (Continued from 94P041B)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Diane diPrima, Allen Ginsberg, and Anne Waldman reading, July, 1994.

docs.creator: Thomas, Lorenzo
docs.description: Lorenzo Thomas lectures on racial identity and its literary representation. Arguing that ethnicity in contemporary America is a politically utilitarian fiction, Thomas discusses the history of ethnicity as concept and representation in American literature. He presents a view of African-American poetry as a reflection of historically changing self-definitions using poems by African-American authors, from Phyllis Wheatley to Amiri Baraka, to illustrate those changes. In the question and answer period, students and faculty discuss definitions of the mainstream, how to write about identity, and the projection of contemporary attitudes about race into the distant past. Thomas closes by reading his poem, "Rhumba Negro."
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Lorenzo Thomas lecture on racial identity and its literary representation, July, 1997.

docs.creator: Moore, Thurston
docs.description: Recorded March, 9th, 2006 at the Boulder Theater, Thurston Moore of Sonic Youth performs his poetry and music as part of a benifit for Burma Life and La Casa de la Esperanza. For the first half of the recording, Thrurston reads poems from his books, Alabama Wildman, What I like About Feminism and Nice War, the latter two in their entirety. The second half is a set of songs mostly from the Sonic Youth Ep, Rather Ripped (release date, June 2006) including, Lights Out, Incinerate, Sleeping Around, Pink Steam, and Or. The final song is a colloaboration with ealier performers, Strangers Die Everyday (see D-06-0003) titled, Walrus. Thurston Moore plays guitar and recites, They are Bombing the Garden of Eden, a poem by James Broughtan (1913-1999).
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Thurston Moore performance March 2006

docs.creator: Moore, LeRoy
docs.description: This is tape 1 of a LeRoy Moore lecture on the history and theory of nonviolence. Moore talks about a few examples of nonviolent figures in history including Ghandi and MLK Jr. He describes Ghandi's theory on the three reactions to violence, Johann Galtung's personal and structural violence with examples of violent social structures and how modern structure fits into this. Moore also notes feminist influences on the theory of non-violence and the connection between property owning and violent action.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: LeRoy Moore class part 1 June 1986

docs.creator: Osman, Jena
docs.description: A lecture, "Anne Waldman as Performer And Collaborator," given by Jena Osman at Naropa University July 1 2003. Osman's lecture is centered on Anne Waldman as collaborator. Osman discusses Waldman's collaboration with such figures as Richard Tuttle, Akilah Oliver, Reed Bye, Bob Dylan et al. Osman plays recordings (film clips, CD's) of Waldman reading and performing various works.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Lecture by Jena Osman on Anne Waldman July 2003

docs.creator: Warsh, Lewis
docs.description: Lewis Warsh class on the autobiography in writing. The class covers composition of poetry and prose, letters and biography in a range of workd including Gurtrude Stein, Kenneth Koch, and his own compositions in dealing with the autobiographical in writing. This is part 1 of 3.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Lewis Warsh class part 1 June 1978

docs.creator: Schelling, Andrew
docs.description: Andrew Schelling lectures on the relationship between environmentalism and Buddhist philosophy and poetry. He begins with the Jataka stories about the Buddha's previous incarnations, including many stories about the Buddha's kindness to animals. He also discusses the Ramayana, or "first poem" in Indian poetry. Schelling relates Buddhist doctrines and practices involving compassion for animals to the environmental movements in the United States and India, including the Chipko movement and Earth First!, as well as Ghandi's concept of Ahimsa.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Andrew Schelling lecture, A garland for environmentalists, July, 1990.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: A class by Philip Whalen in July, 1976. Whalen lectures on "the particular minute" thinking of Emily Dickinson. He also talks about two of his own poems, "Matchbox" and "Mind is simple, art is shapely." Part 1 of a two-part class. Part 2 is on 76P069-070.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class, part 1, July, 1976.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: A class, "Rotating Shakespeare," taught by Philip Whalen at the Naropa Institute August 8, 1980. Whalen continues his lecture and discussion into Shakespeare's play Pericles. Whalen opens the class us for discussion. This is part 2 of 3.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class part 2 August 1980

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: A class, "Rotating Shakespeare," taught by Philip Whalen at the Naropa Institute August 8, 1980. Whalen continues discussing Pericles and Shakespeare in general. This is part 3 of 3.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class part 3 August 1980

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: Second half of a Philip Whalen class on the history of little magazines, their rebirth and proliferation beginning in the late 1940's, and their importance as a way for writers to communicate. He talks about his experience of being published in a little magazine and reads and discusses many examples of poetry, interviews, and other material from them. Magazines discussed include The Little Magazine of America, The Little Review, Bruno's Bohemia, The Poetry Book Magazine, Gregory Corso's Cambridge Review, Ed Sanders's Fuck You: A Magazine of the Arts, Simon Schuchat's Four Three Two Review, Dodgems, and Ted Berrigan's C Magazine, among others. (Continued from 77P031)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class, part 8, August 1977.

docs.creator: Cope, David; Rakosi, Carl
docs.description: David Cope divers poems ranging from Vietnam, Immigration, and Fishing. Carl Rakosi, an Objectivist poet, draws haunting meditaions on the movement of age and culture.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Cope and Rakosi read part 1

docs.creator: Wilson, Peter Lamborn
docs.description: First half of part 2, of a two-part class, by Peter Lamborn Wilson on utopian poetics. Students read assigned utopian poetic statements and discuss with Wilson points that arose in those statements. Topics covered include science fiction, scientific paradigms, and the notion of progress; Nietzsche's ubermensch and society of free spirits; Bardism vs. much of contemporary American poetry; cooptation of creativity into the spectacle and how to evade it; normative education in America; and the importance and fragility of artistic community. (Continues on 93P069)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Peter Lamborn Wilson class, Utopian poetics, part 2, July, 1993.

docs.creator: Kapil Rider, Bhanu; Mullen, Laura; Polito, Robert; Yau, John
docs.description: A prose panel from week 3 of the Summer Writing Program at Naropa in 2002, featuring Robert Polito the art of Jim Thompson discussing briefly Ida Lupino, Jim Thompson & the WPA and on the composition of his book on Thompson, Savage Beauty, ending with brief note on Bob Dylan's Time out of Mind and Love and Theft. Laura Mullen reads a cycle of vignettes on composition. John Yau reads an essay on Andy Worhol titled, "Double Self-Portrait." This panel is followed with a Q&A session focused on the sentence and fragmentation, collage and biography. This event continues on 02P054 and is tape 1 of 2.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Prose panel with Rider, Polito, Mullen part 1 June 2002

docs.creator: Baraka, Amiri
docs.description: Second half of a class by Amiri Baraka on revolution and art. Subjects include Harlem Renaissance, American modernism, Langston Hughes, William Carlos Williams, music composition, and a discussion of his murdered sister. Works by the class are also included in the discussion. (Continued from 85p088.) Keywords: New American Poetry, Black Arts Movement, New York School, sound poetry, music in literature, political poetry
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Amiri Baraka class on revolution and art.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: A class by Philip Whalen in Allen Ginsberg's "Spontaneous Poetics" series. Whalen discusses Ben Jonson, primitive peoples and poetries, and names. (Continued on 76p062). Keyword: New American Poetry, West Coast poetry, preliterate culture, oral literature, Buddhism
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class in Allen Ginsberg's spontaneous poetics series.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: First half of Class 8 of "In the Pressure Tank" series held at Naropa Institute between July 23 and August 20, 1980. (The whole series is contained on 80P093-115.) Philip Whalen discusses Wallace Stevens's poem "Academic Discourse at Havana." Specific attention is given to French poets--Stephane Mallarme, Paul Valery, Andre Gide, and others--who influenced Stevens. (Continues on 80p106.) Keywords: New American Poetry, West Coast poetry, Buddhism, American modernist poetry, symbolism
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: In the pressure tank, Class 8

docs.creator: McClure, Michael; Taylor, Steven
docs.description: A Michael McClure and Steven Taylor performance. McClure reads from his book Huge Dreams and performs Zen poems with musical accompaniment by Steven Taylor.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Michael McClure and Steven Taylor performance, June, 1999.

docs.creator: Guravich, Donald; Hollo, Anselm; Jarnot, Lisa; Prevallet, Kristin
docs.description: July 3, 2001 Faculty Reading with Donald Guravich, Lisa Jarnot, Anselm Hollo and Kristin Prevallet. The reading opens with Anne Waldman introducing Mary Kite who presents a small explanation of the Naropa Audio Archive and the level of its importance to the community. Donald Guravich reads a number of pieces including: "Education," "Bob's new career," "Sally and Stan," "Raph the artist" and "Paper and rocks." Lisa Jarnot reads a number of her pieces from her book "Ring of Fire." Kristin Prevellat reads "The voice variously heard," an excerpt from "The Parasite Poems" and "The People's Database." Anselm Hollo reads excerpts from "Guests in Space."
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Faculty Reading: Guravich, Jarnot, Hollo and Prevallet. July 2001.

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: Allen Ginsberg concludes his reading at the Naropa Institute, featuring "Sincerity rap" and a notebook entry for the day of the reading, 7/21/1985.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Ginsberg reading Sincerity rap July 1985

docs.creator: Berssenbrugge, Mei-Mei; Ducornet, Rikki
docs.description: Reading at Naropa University, featuring Rikki Ducornet reading from her novel Gazelle and Mei Mei Berssenbrugge reading from Nest and the long poem "Safety." This is part 2 of 2.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Faculty reading with Ducornet, Berssenbrugge part 2 July 2003

docs.description: naropa
docs.title: Faculty reading with Kizershot Bye part 1, June 2002

docs.creator: Aebi, Irene; Lacy, Steve
docs.description: First half of a class with Irene Aebi and Steve Lacy discussing the formation of the Art Song Trio. There is discussion about the difficulties of writing music to accompany a poem. Lacy and Aebi illustrate this point using a series called "Nine love songs." A recording from the series titled "You want to know" is played. Several other recordings are played including "I'm out," "Remark," "In the great monotony," "To marry," and "Pine." (Continues on 01P094)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Irene Aebi and Steve Lacy class, Nine love songs, July, 2001.
Frakest and Frechette Reading

docs.creator: Snyder, Gary
docs.description: 83p067 and 83p068 constitute a class in series of classes with Gary Snyder in which Snyder discusses "The Book of Songs", his poems, the importance of saying grace, the role of the poet in society, and visions.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Gary Snyder Book of Songs class part 2 1983

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: This is an odd tape project on one side of a tape that appears to be a private conversation between Ginsberg and other artists that are not names. The conversation is interupted by Phone Calls and abruptly ends. There is a long silence and then there are two songs that are poorly produced that are not given names. Both f these songs appear on the album "Capitol Raspberry". The tape ends in mid-lyric.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Ginsberg and Capitol Record 1981

docs.creator: Coolidge, Clark; Creeley, Robert; Lacy, Steve; Mackey, Nathaniel
docs.description: First half of a panel on jazz featuring Clark Coolidge, Steve Lacy, Nathaniel Mackey, and Robert Creeley. Coolidge, who worked as a jazz drummer at one time, begins by reading his piece, "A note on bop." The panelists move on to a discussion of bop as a language, rhythm, the relationship of words to music, and their own experiences with jazz. They also touch briefly on the work of Harry Partch. (Continues on 91P066)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Clark Coolidge, Robert Creeley and Steve Lacy panel, Poetry and jazz, July, 1991.

docs.creator: Sanchez, Sonia; Taylor, Steven; Torres, Edwin; Waldman, Anne; Wellman, Mac
docs.description: Opening panel from week four of the 2003 Summer Writing Program. The topic is "Performance and Collaboration." The panel includes Sonia Sanchez, Mac Wellman and Edwin Torres with chair Steven Taylor. Highlights include discussion of the potential of performance and collaboration, Sonia Sanchez on the limiting of labeling performances according to genre and race, Mac Wellman on "the hoax" as a genre of writing, and a discussion of the social responsibility of the poet.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Sonjia Sanchez, Steven Taylor, Edwin Torres, Anne Waldman, and Mac Wellman panel on perfomance and collaboration, June, 2003.

docs.creator: Wilson, Peter Lamborn
docs.description: First half of a Peter Lamborn Wilson lecture about the art of Sufi traveling. He focuses on travel in the world of Islam, discussing the history of nomadic travel and tradition. He relates several anecdotes about Ibn Arabi and recites a Sufi traveling song. (Continues on 91P150)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Peter Lamborn Wilson lecture, Sacred drift: the art of Sufi travel, July, 1991.

docs.creator: Bye, Reed
docs.description: A short talk by Reed Bye on the increasing mindfulness that comes from dharma practice, including a question and answer session.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Reed Bye, Dharma talk, June, 1988.

docs.creator: Field, Thalia; Myles, Eileen; Pate, Alexs
docs.description: This is reading given during the summer of 2000 with Thalia Field, Alexs Pate, and Eileen Myles. In this reading there is a variety of prose and poetry best showing what they were working on at the time.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Reading with Field, Pate, Myles June 2000

docs.creator: Grenier, Robert
docs.description: Robert Grenier on language part 4 July 1992. Grenier reads poetry by Kenneth Irby, references works by Ezra pound, and D. H. Lawrence and discusses the relation of language to place.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Robert Grenier on language part 4 July 1992

docs.creator: Blaser, Robin; Hawkins, Bobbie Louise; Myles, Eileen; Oliver, Akilah; Schelling, Andrew; Tejada, Roberto
docs.description: First half of a Naropa Summer Writing Program faculty reading, featuring poetry by Roberto Tejado and Robin Blaser, prose by Bobbie Louise Hawkins, and poetry and prose by Eileen Myles. (Continued on 01P055)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Robing Blaser, Bobbi Loiuse Hawkins, Eileen Myles, and Akila Oliver reading, June 2001.

docs.creator: Blaser, Robin; Schelling, Andrew
docs.description: Part two of a two part lecture series by Robin Blaser entitled Belief, doubt, and politics. Blaser discusses language, spirituality, sexuality, gender and the existential given. He reads and discusses the ideas and writing of Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Stephane Mallarme and chiasmatic language, Frederich Nietzsche's parable "The madman" and his book The Gay Science/The Joyful Wisdom, Jean-Francois Lyotard's book The Postmodern Condition, and Martha Nussbaum's ideas about the soul. Blaser reads several of his own poems, including The outsider, written for the Gay Games in Vancouver.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Robin Blaser lecture, Belief, doubt and politics, Part 2, July, 1992.

docs.creator: Ortiz, Simon
docs.description: Simon Ortiz reads poems and sings songs from several books and manuscripts, including his books From Sand Creek, Going for the Rain, and Big Mountain: The People and Land Are Sacred.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Simon Ortiz reading, May, 1984.

docs.creator: Aebi, Irene; Elmslie, Kenward; Lacy, Steve; Owen, Maureen; Patton, Julie; Taylor, Steven; Torres, Edwin; Waldman, Anne; Welish, Marjorie
docs.description: A panel on visual arts and performance chaired by Anne Waldman. Panelists Marjorie Welish, Maureen Owen, Edwin Torres, Steve Lacy, Irene Aebi, Kenward Elmslie, Julie Patton, and Steven Taylor make individual statements about the relationships between the creative arts and respond to questions from the audience. The panelists discuss their performance and collaboration work in writing, music, and other art forms. Several panelists place themselves in a historical context, discussing their relationship to earlier artists ranging from Homer to the New York jazz scene in the 1960s and 1970s. The event includes Marjorie Welish reading and discussing John Taggart's poem "Slow song for Mark Rothko," as well as Kenward Elmslie and Steven Taylor performing Elmslie's songs "Eggs," and "And I was there." (Continued on 82P083)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anne Waldman, Marjorie Welish, Maureen Owen, Edwin Torres, Steve Lacy, Irene Aebi, Kenward Elmslie, Julie Patton, and Steven Taylor panel, July, 2001.

docs.creator: Taylor, Steven
docs.description: First half of a Steven Taylor workshop on music. Taylor begins by talking about music, consciousness, the human ear, and neurology. He plays and discusses a wide variety of examples of music from many different eras and places including African, Tibetan, European chants, Jimi Hendrix, opera, troubadour songs and Moon Dog. (Continues on 91P131)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Steven Taylor workshop, Music and consciousness, July, 1991.

docs.creator: Waldman, Anne
docs.description: First half of an Anne Waldman class, continuing her series from the summer of 1977 on women writers. This is one of the final classes, discussing the lives of Marianne Moore, Rebecca Brown, Lorine Niedecker, and Jane Bowels. Waldman reads selections from the writers' works. There is also a discussion of future classes, and a question and answer session. (Continues on 77P077)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anne Waldman class, Women Writers, August, 1977.

docs.creator: Allen Ginsberg
docs.description: Allen Ginsberg course on 19th Century Poetics: William Blake. This portion of the class continues from the previous tape 81P164 talking about "The Mental Travelor" and its relation to "The Four Zoas." There is much discussion by AG leading the class through line by line of the readings with explantions of characters and Blake's interpretation of life and its meaning and imagination.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg Class 19th Century Poetry, part 8

docs.creator: Schelling, Andrew
docs.description: Second half of an Andrew Schelling class on the poetic and literary traditions of indigenous peoples and how poetry and music are used for healing in indigenous societies. He talks about how indigenous societies have been damaged by contact with industrialized nations and discusses the concept of shamanism. He describes various types of indigenous literature including love songs, work songs, healing rituals, and magical incantations, relating them to musical and literary traditions in American culture such as the blues, Dada, protest music, and Beat poetry. (Continued from 90P001)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Andrew Schelling lecture on tribal politics and songs of healing, July, 1990.

docs.creator: Vicuna, Cecilia
docs.description: Cecilia Vicuna gives a lecture on Word and Thread. She opens with a chant and then leads into a discussion of language and the various forms in which it manifests. Examples include textile, line and word. She traces the origin of many words including: polvo, order, line and nombre. There are many references to Andian Quechua culture and the quipo. The lecture closes and is followed by many students questions. July 15, 1994.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Cecilia Vicuna Lecture Word and Thread July 1994

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: Second half of a class with Philip Whalen discussing 17th and 18th century English literature and worldview, focusing on the works of James Boswell, Ben Jonson, Jonathan Swift, and Alexander Pope. (Continued from 84p044.) Keywords: New American Poetry, West Coast poetry, Buddhism, 17th and 18th century literature
docs.title: Philip Whalen class on 18th century literature - Part 2

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: Allen Ginsberg discusses the importance of and references in Jack Kerouac's Mexico City Blues. Plays significant portion of a reading Kerouac did, accompanied by a jazz pianist.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Ginsberg Mexico City Blues July 1988

docs.description: no description
docs.title: Naropa Archive 1

docs.creator: Waldman, Anne
docs.description: This tape is of a Gertrude Stein Marathon reading. It is the second of two tapes that includes Naropa students and faculty performing poems and a play by Stein. Performed works include "Short Sentances," "History Slowly", "As a Wife Has a Cow: A Love Story," and Making of Americans."(89P099)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Marathon Reading July 1989

docs.creator: Baraka, Amiri; Ginsberg, Allen; Kyger, Joanne; Waldman, Anne; Wilson, Peter Lamborn
docs.description: First half of a panel on counter-poetics and opposition with Anne Waldman, Joanne Kyger, Amiri Baraka, Allen Ginsberg, and Peter Lamborn Wilson. Waldman begins by reading an excerpt from Columbus's journal describing how easy it will be to exploit the people of the Americas. She proposes a program for incorporating political activism into poetics. The panelists make individual statements about counter-poetics and move to more open discussion. They propose definitions for the term and look at how to be oppositional in relation to racism, eurocentrism, and political oppression. The panel includes a reading by Peter Lamborn Wilson of his sermonette "Critique of the listener." (Continues on 92P144)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Panel on counter-poetics and opposition, July, 1992.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: Philip Whalen lectures on writing and seeing. He begins by talking about his experience at the Tassajara Zen Mountain Center and goes on to discuss John Locke's ideas about how people convey their experience to others. He also refers to the thinking of Bishop Berkeley, Laurence Sterne, Charles Olson, and Allen Ginsberg. Whalen reads and discusses some of his writing,including his poem "Apple gravy" and part of his novel You Didn't Even Try. The lecture ends with a question and answer session.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class, part 1, August, 1977.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: A class, "Rotating Shakespeare," taught by Philip Whalen August 6, 1980. Whalen speaks at length about the historical circumstances of Shakespeare's play Pericles. Whalen spends the majority of the class reading from the play. This is part 1 of 3.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class part 1 August 1980

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: First half of a class by Philip Whalen from August 1977. Shakespeare, John Donne, and Ben Johnson are topics of discussion. Also The Japanese and Japanese culture are presented. (Continues on 77P026)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class, part 2, August 1977.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: Second half of a class by Philip Whalen during the summer of 1976 . Whalen reads and discusses the work of Walt Whitman, Herman Melville, Henry James and Henry David Thoreau. Whitman's preface to his book, Leaves of Grass, his essay "Democratic vistas" and sections from his book, Specimen Days, are used to assess the intersection of American political, economic, social and poetic potential and realities.(Continued from 76P069)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class, part 2, July, 1976.

docs.creator: Warshall, Peter
docs.description: Peter Warshall lectures on a poetics of natural light. Warshall explains light and sight from a biologist's standpoint, showing how they are part of a several billion year process of evolution. He explicates the connections between survival and elements of light perception, including contrast, concealment, and color. Warshall sees art as a development of the uses of these elements in the animal kingdom, and relates the artist's and poet's search for beauty to the naturalist's.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Peter Warshall lecture, A Poetics of Natural Light, June, 1996.

docs.creator: Snyder, Gary
docs.description: Gary Snyder class. Snyder discusses tips for writing poetry, several editing processes, and some Japanese Zen literary advice. He also reads several translations of Chinese poems, talks about Gregory Bateson and Wendell Barry, and reads Kenneth Roxroth's translation of a poem called "Full Moon."
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Gary Snyder Class poetry August 1983

docs.creator: Burke, Junior; Guravich, Donald; Hunt, Laird
docs.description: A reading from June of 2003. Performers on this tape are Junior Burke and Donald Guravich. Burke sings a combination of Philip Whalen's "Dear Mister President" and a mass e-mail of President Bush's resume and reads from his novel, "Us." Guravich reads numerous poems including, "Artifacts," "The Patriot Act," and, "The Best Movie Ever Made." Continues on 03P070
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Faculty Reading with Coultas, Bye, Burke, Guravich part 1 June 2003

docs.creator: Mullen, Laura; Polito, Robert
docs.description: Robert Polito reads "Barbara Payton, A Memoir." Laura Mullen reads from "Demonstrating Bodies."
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Faculty reading with Polito, Mullen June 2002

docs.creator: Berssenbrugge, Mei-Mei; Kyger, Joanne; Osman, Jena; Perelman, Bob
docs.description: First half of a poetry reading with Jena Osman, Bob Perelman, Mei Mei Bersenbrugge, and Joanne Kyger. Osman reads from "Press scrutiny." Bersennbrugge reads from her book, Nest, and Perelman reads "Fake dream: the library," "Today's lament," "Ode to James Fennimore Cooper," and others. (Continues on 01P026)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Jena Osman, Bob Perelman, Mei Mei Bersenbrugge, and Joanne Kyger reading, June, 2001.

docs.creator: Rothenberg, Jerome
docs.description: Jerome Rothenberg class on ethnopoetics and performance, discussing balance and sanity in the Marakami, Don Genaro in Castaneda, poverty and cultural richness, ceremonies and political change, Native Americans in relation to settled areas and wilderness, Maria Sabina on women and shamanism followed by a movie about her, Sabina's account of the first cure and shamans as mediums. Part 3 of a series.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Jerome Rothenberg class on ethnopoetics and performance, August, 1981, part 3.

docs.creator: Waldman, Anne
docs.description: First half of an Ann Waldman class on spirit in poetry. Waldman discusses the relationship between poetry and the sacred. She draws on a wide variety of material, including the work of Ted Berrigan, Charles Olson, Sumerian mythology, Dante, and Buddhist treasure texts.(Continues on 89P034)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anne Waldman class, Spirit in poetry, July, 1989.

docs.creator: Waldman, Anne
docs.description: First half of an Anne Waldman class. Waldman discusses the poets Arthur Rimbaud, Ezra Pound, Emily Dickenson, and Sappho. There is also a question and answer session. (Continues on 86P039)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anne Waldman class, Word women, June, 1986.

docs.creator: Waldman, Anne
docs.description: Second half of an Anne Waldman lecture on the use of the cut-up technique in the work of William S. Burroughs, tracing it from its early development through his later work. She reads from Burroughs's writing and an interview with him in The Paris Review, plays his cut-up tapes, and talks about how Burroughs extended the idea of cut-ups beyond writing to a way of understanding the universe in magical and mystical terms. (Continued from 85P067)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anne Waldman lecture on William S. Burroughs's cut-up method, July, 1985.

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: This is a class on Shakespeare's Tempest, taught by Allen Ginsberg, from August 20, 1980 at Naropa. At the outset, Ginsberg explains that instead of reading the whole play through, he will touch on important lines in each Act and scene and explore them deeply. In this recording he discusses Act III scenes 1 through 3 with various digressions and explications on Shakespeare's metaphores. This is class 3 of 4.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg class 3

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: Second half of an Allen Ginsberg class on writing poetry. He begins by referring to William Carlos Williams's exhortation, "No ideas but in things," comparing it to Chogyam Trungpa Rinpoche's statement that "Things are symbols of themselves." He reads from Shakespeare's poetry to illustrate his point. During the lecture, Ginsberg also touches on Haiku, Kerouac, and other topics. (Continued from 84P022)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg class, On writing poetry, July, 1984.

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: Allen Ginsberg lecture on expansive poetics, focusing on the influences of Walt Whitman. He discusses Surrealism, Albert Einstein, Whitman, Federico Garcia Lorca, Paul Klebnikov, Christopher Smart, Ezra Pound, William Carlos Williams, Hart Crane and Edgar Allen Poe. Ginsberg reads Lorca's "Ode to Salvador Dali," Whitman's "Reversals," "Respondez" and "Crossing Brooklyn Ferry," Klebnikov's "Menagerie," Smart's "Rejoice of the lamb," and Crane's "The river."
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg lecture on expansive poetics, Sons of Whitman, June, 1981.

docs.creator: Berkson, Bill
docs.description: A class, "Transmitting," taught by Bill Berkson at the Naropa Institute June 21, 1978. Among the various topics covered in Berkson's lecture: D.H. Lawrence, Rudy Burkhardt, Willem de Kooning, Clark Coolidge, John Cage, Alex Katz and Charles Reznikoff. Berkson also reads and discusses his poem "Negative." This is class 2 of 2.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Bill Berkson class 2 June 1978

docs.creator: Augustine, Jane; Heller, Michael; Hollo, Anselm
docs.description: A reading with Jane Augustine, Michael Heller, and Ansel Hollo. Each reads many of their own poems. Augustine focuses somewhat on mountains.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Augustine Heller Hollo Reading

docs.creator: Coolidge, Clark
docs.description: Second half of a Michael McClure and Clark Coolidge reading. Coolidge concludes his reading of his poem, "American Ones." (Continued from 77P106)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Clark Coolidge and Michael McClure reading, July, 1977.

docs.creator: Rakosi, Carl
docs.description: Second half of a Carl Rakosi reading of an interview with himself by an unknown interviewer. The question and answer session continues. (Continued from 87P023)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Carl Rakosi reading of an interview with himself, July, 1987.

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: Second half of a class on the history of poetry by Allen Ginsberg, from a series of classes during the summer of 1975. Ginsberg discusses the poets William Carlos Williams, Gregory Corso and Jack Kerouac. He includes several personal anecdotes about the poets and reads selections from their works. A class discussion follows. (Continued from 75P020A)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg class, The history of poetry, part 19, June, 1975.

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: First half of an Allen Ginsberg lecture on English and American lyric poetry. Ginsberg reads William Blake's "Let the brothels of paris be opened," "The gray monk," "The Mask of anarchy," "The ballad of Sir Patrick Spense," "The Holy land of walsingham" and "Weep you no more, sad fountains," followed by Thomas Wyatt's "My lute awake," "Forget not yet," "They flee from me," "Gasgoyne's lullaby" and "Tickborn's elegy." (Continues on 96P050)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg lecture on English and American lyric poetry, July, 1996.

docs.creator: Carroll, Jim; Waldman, Anne
docs.description: Second half of a poetry reading with Jim Carroll and Anne Waldman. Waldman reads "Skin meat bones," "All hollow's eve" (with flute accompaniment), "Sisters," "A dialogue between a silicon child and a clematis flower" (with saxophone accompaniment), "Too bad trains," "The tundra and the waves," "You're like ice" (with drums and gourd accompaniment) and "Anarchy." (Continued from 86P085)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anne Waldman and Jim Carroll reading, July, 1986.

docs.creator: Waldman, Anne
docs.description: An Anne Waldman class, "Poet as Shaman," part 2. The works of poets Frank O'Hara and Charles Olson are discussed along with the ideas of poems as journeys or other worlds, and dreaming and butterfly imagery in the poetry of Chang-Tzu. (Series continues on 79P032)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anne Waldman class, Poet as shaman, part 2, July, 1979.

docs.creator: McClure, Michael
docs.description: Second half of a Michael McClure lecture about the origins of theater. He discusses the relationship between plays and poetry, his concept of "beast language" and his own plays, "The feast," "The beard" and "Josephine the mouse singer." (Continued from 89P133)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Michael McClure lecture about the origins of theater, July, 1989.

docs.creator: Ducornet, Rikki
docs.description: Recorded July 3rd, 1999 at Naropa, Rikki Ducornet reads her four part essay on Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels. The essay covers the catalogical, misogynistic, and scatalogical elements in Swift's work. After reading her essay she answers questions from the audience.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Rikki Ducornet Optical Terror July 1999

docs.creator: Tallman, Warren
docs.description: Warren Tallman contrasts the attitude toward language of the poets of the modern period (which he defines as spanning 1600 to 1900) and those of the postmodern period (spanning in his definition 1900 to the present), and prophesies the imminent return of "personal poetry" to the fore. Using examples from Chaucer, Yeats and Donne, Tallman proposes that consonants lead the mind to speech, while vowels lead it to song. Other topics covered include Freud and Jung (including a discussion of the idea of synchronicity), Buddhism and poetry (a subject on which we hear Ginsberg's opinion), and the clusters of poems written by Ginsberg and Creeley in the Bay Area in the 1950's.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Warren Tallman class 1986

docs.creator: Warshall, Peter
docs.description: Peter Warshall lectures on water. Warshall narrates the scientific story of the origin of water on Earth, in four stages. He then describes the molecular structure of water and how it illustrates love: covalent bonds illustrate the strong bond of equal sharing; ionic bonds illustrate the weaker bond of relatedness and openness; and surface tension illustrates the principles of resiliency and light touch, receptivity and boundaries. Warshall concludes with a discussion of "The water contract" and ecological interdependence. In the question and answer session, he discusses water purity and the effects of mineral content on the behavior of water.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Peter Warshall lecture on water, June, 1995.

docs.creator: Waldman, Anne
docs.description: An Anne Waldman reading at Naropa University on an unknown date. Waldman reads "Crack in the world," and "Pieces of an hour."
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anne Waldman reading, Crack in the world, Pieces of an hour, Date not available.

docs.creator: Bye, Reed; Ginsberg, Allen; Waldman, Anne
docs.description: Reed Bye reads pieces including "Life and Death," "Life and Death," and "Simple House," and "To a Prisoner Waiting." Anne Waldman reads pieces including "Stones," "Waiting," and "Animals." Allen Ginsberg reads his "Ode to Failure," a Sapphic poem, and "Classical Bathtub Thoughts" among others. continued from 80P171
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Poetry Reading with Bye Waldman Ginsberg May 1980

docs.creator: Waldman, Anne
docs.description: First half of an Anne Waldman lecture on the use of the cut-up technique in the work of William S. Burroughs, tracing it from its early development through his later work. She reads from Burroughs's writing and an interview with him in The Paris Review, plays his cut-up tapes, and talks about how Burroughs extended the idea of cut-ups beyond writing to a way of understanding the universe in magical and mystical terms. (Continued on 85P068)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anne Waldman lecture on William S. Burroughs's cut-up method, July, 1985.

docs.creator: Abbott, Keith; Ping, Wang; Thomas, Lorenzo
docs.description: First half of a reading by Keith Abbot, Wang Ping, and Lorenzo Thomas. Abbott reads "Zabioni," "What you know with no name for it," "Doing it to death," and others. Ping reads "Flash of selfish consciousness" and "8000 miles of clouds and rains." Thomas reads "Morning raga," "The sadness of space exploration," "The midnight sun," "An education" and "Hollandaise salsa." (Continues on 97P036)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Keith Abbott, Wang Ping, and Lorenzo Thomas reading, July, 1997.

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: A literature class, "Basic Poetics," taught by Allen Ginsberg May 26, 1980. Ginsberg begins the class by singing poems by Sappho and songs by William Blake and Isaac Watts accompanied by harmonium. The rest of the class is devoted to Christopher Smart's poetry, specifically "Rejoice In The Lamb" and "Jubilate Agno." This is class 32 of 33.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg Basic Poetics class 32

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: A reading by Allen Ginsberg performing William Blake's Songs of Innocence and Songs of Experience. Songs of Innocence includes: "The Shepherd," "The Echoing Green," "The Lamb," "The Little Black Boy," "The Blossom," "The Chimney Sweeper," "The Little Boy Lost," "The Little Boy Found," "Laughing Song," and "Holy Thursday." Songs of Experience includes: "Nurse's Song," "The Sick Rose," "Ah Sunflower," "The Garden of Love," "London," "The Human Abstract," "To Tirzah" and "The Grey Monk." Keywords: New American Poetry, beat movement, visionary poetry, music in literature, performance poetry
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg performing William Blake.

docs.creator: Collom, Jack; Mayer, Bernadette
docs.description: An energetic reading by Jack Collom of his work. He reads a few pieces of various lengths - relatively short to quite long.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Collom reading

docs.creator: Gladman, Renee; Hollo, Anselm; Mullen, Harryette; Sikelianos, Eleni
docs.description: A reading by Anselm Hollo, from "Guests of space," and Harryette Mullen, from "Sleeping with the dictionary." Partial readings include Eleni Sikelianos and Renee Gladman, which are cut off during the recording process.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anselm Hollo, Haryette Mullen, Renee Gladman, and Eleni Sikelianos reading, June, 2002.

docs.creator: Patton, Julie
docs.description: A Julie Patton performance, "Boulder: an opera," a rock opera performance piece with spoken word and backbround music, performed at the Boulder opera house.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Julie Patton performance, Boulder, an opera, July, 1998.

docs.creator: Gladman, Renee; Hawkins, Bobbie Louise; Hunt, Laird; Kapil Rider, Bhanu
docs.description: A panel with Bobbie Louise Hawkins, Bhanu Kapil Rider, Renee Gladman, Laird Hunt, and members of the audience in a wide ranging discussion of writing fiction across cultures, personally and within narratives; how that fiction can be received; objectivity; and our currently multimedia-ed, overpopulated world.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Panel with Bobbie Louise Hawkins, Renee Gladman, Laird Hunt and Bhanu Kapil Rider.

docs.creator: Delany, Samuel R.; Yamashita, Karen Tei; Zivancevic, Nina
docs.description: Second half of a panel focusing on problems associated with the translation of prose, both within one's own language and from or to other languages. Samuel R. Delany says translation is always a matter of paraphrase and of negotiating language and communication. Nina Zivancevic discusses the impossibility of translating some words and therefore, some literature. Karen Tei Yamashita discusses the diaspora of language and memory. The panel also includes a question and answer session. (Continued from 02P010.)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Panel on the problems of prose translation, June, 2001.

docs.creator: Rowan, Peter; Taylor, Steven
docs.description: First part of a Peter Rowan and Steven Taylor performance at the Naropa Institute. Taylor opens with classical guitar music. Rowan plays "Cowboys and Indians," "Wondering," "On a dusty old road," "The free Mexican airforce," "Cool springs," "Like a moth to a flame," "If you fallin'," "O here I go again," "The walls of time" and "Thirsty in the rain." (Continued on 87P028 and 87P029)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Peter Rowan and Steven Taylor performance, July, 1987.

docs.creator: Grenier, Robert
docs.description: The fourth tape in a series of five containing a class taught by Robert Grenier. Subject matter of the class includes the work of Joanne Kyger as well as that of Kenneth Irby.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Robert Grenier on language part 3 July 1992

docs.creator: Burroughs, William S.
docs.description: Second half of a workshop with William S. Burroughs comparing his works to those of Jack Kerouac and discussing their writing techniques. Burroughs provides biographical information on meeting Kerouac and their ensuing relationship. He also discusses what it means to be a writer, and how many people are not writers even though they claim to be and have published work. Burroughs responds to questions about his relationship with Kerouac, dreams, and his own literary influences. (Continued from 82P267A)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: On the road: Jack Kerouac Conference, William S. Burroughs workshop, July, 1982.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: A class by Philip Whalen in Allen Ginsberg's "Spontaneous Poetics" series. Whalen discusses Ben Jonson, primitive peoples and poetries, and names. (Continued from 76p061). Keyword: New American Poetry, West Coast poetry, preliterate culture, oral literature, Buddhism
docs.title: Philip Whalen class n Allen Ginsberg's spontaneous poetics series.

docs.creator: Acker, Kathy; Brownstein, Michael
docs.description: First half of a Kathy Acker and Michael Brownstein reading. Brownstein reads a selection of poems, including "Paris Visitation," "Distance Between People," and "Breakdown On Broadway." Kathy Acker selections include "Sex Show." (Continues on 79P097)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Kathy Acker and Michael Brownstein reading, June, 1979.

docs.creator: Palmer, Michael
docs.description: A lecture by Michael Palmer exploring translation and its aesthetic implications. The title refers to writers who refuse to submit to an authoritarian poetic or political reality. Palmer discusses Arthur Rimbaud, Herman Melville, Stephane Mallarme, Friedrich Holderlin ,Octavio Paz and Paul Celan. The lecture concludes with a brief question and answer session.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Michael Palmer lecture, Bad to the bone: What I learned outside, June, 2002.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: Second half of a class with Philip Whalen discussing Alexander Pope's life, and the cultural context of his work. Whalen reads and discusses several works by Pope, including "The Heathen to His Departing Soul," "The Dying Christian to His Soul," "A Rondeau," "An Epistle to a Doctor of Divinity...," and "The Dunciad." (Continued from 84p042.) Keywords: New American Poetry, West Coast poetry, Buddhism, 17th and 18th century literature
docs.title: Philip Whalen class on Alexander Pope - Part 2

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: First half of part 3 of an Allen Ginsberg workshop series on American value. Ginsberg reads several poems as examples of the mind in operation, and talks about how poetry can arise from meditation practice and ordinary mind. He reads and discusses the work of Charles Reznikoff, William Carlos Williams, and other writers. (Continues on 87P084)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg class, American value, part 3, March, 1987.

docs.creator: Coolidge, Clark
docs.description: A class, "Rotating Shakespeare," taught by Clark Coolidge at the Naropa Institute July 2, 1980. Coolidge finishes reading Timon Of Athens to the class culminating with Q & A session. This is part 4 of 4.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Clark Coolidge class part 4 July 1980

docs.creator: Wilson, Peter Lamborn
docs.description: Second half of a Peter Lamborn Wilson lecture on hermetic linguistics. Wilson discusses schools of thinking based on a mistrust of words, including Nietzsche's anti-linguistics, The Will to Power, and John Zerzan's Elements of Refusal. He looks at modernist and avant-garde poetry as an assault on language. Wilson also discusses mystical approaches to language, including the map of the cosmos with God-letters at the center, the function of the imagination, the ability of words to shatter concepts, and the use of archetypes. (Continued from 89P142)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Peter Lamborn Wilson class on hermetic linguistics, July, 1989.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: First half of a Philip Whalen class on the history of little magazines, their rebirth and proliferation beginning in the late 1940's, and their importance as a way for writers to communicate. He talks about his experience of being published in a little magazine and reads and discusses many examples of poetry, interviews, and other material from them. Magazines discussed include The Little Magazine of America, The Little Review, Bruno's Bohemia, The Poetry Book Magazine, Gregory Corso's Cambridge Review, Ed Sanders's Fuck You: A Magazine of the Arts, Simon Schuchat's Four Three Two Review, Dodgems, and Ted Berrigan's C Magazine, among others. (Continues on 77P032)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class, part 5, August 1977.

docs.creator: Thomas, Lorenzo
docs.description: Lorenzo Thomas lectures on poetry and social action. He reads and discusses pieces written as social action commentary, such as "By the rivers of Babylon" (Psalm 137), The Declaration of Independence, Frederick Douglass's "What to the American slave is the 4th of July?", and poems by Paul Laurence Dunbar and John Greenleaf Whittier. Thomas also discusses Douglass's life in relation to the abolitionist movement, the civil rights movement, and the current situation in the Middle East.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Lorenzo Thomas lecture, How to see through poetry: myth, perception, and history, July, 2002.

docs.creator: Waldman, Anne
docs.description: A class in a series by Anne Waldman, "Poet as shaman," part 1. Students read and discuss dreams that they have recorded. Also included are discussions of Navajo songs, snake medicine songs, and an all night chant with mushrooms. (Series continues on 79P031)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anne Waldman class, Poet as shaman, part 1, July, 1979.

docs.creator: Whalen, Philip
docs.description: First half of a class with Philip Whalen discussing Alexander Pope's life, and the cultural context of his work. Whalen reads and discusses several works by Pope, including "The Heathen to His Departing Soul," "The Dying Christian to His Soul," "A Rondeau," "An Epistle to a Doctor ofDivinity...," and "The Dunciad." (Continues on 84p043.) Keywords: New American Poetry, West Coast poetry, Buddhism, 17th and 18th century literatur.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Philip Whalen class on Alexander Pope.

docs.creator: Mayer, Bernadette
docs.description: This is the final part of a class that began on 89P091. In this portion of the class students read their crafted poems and discuss their attempts at new form which range from writing and pronouncing words backwards to etymology to using card game instructions to write a poem. The class does begin with an interesting conversation on memory and Giordano Bruno that is a digression from the rest of the content. Series includes 89P075 and 89P092.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Bernadette Mayer workshop part 2
Faculty Reading with Hunt, Mullen, Alcalay

docs.creator: Cope, David
docs.description: David Cope presents a class at the Naropa Institute, July 8, 1980. He focuses on publishing and editing, and the work of Charles Reznikoff. He introduces Reznikoff's writing, his work in Hollywood, and indeterminancy and objectivism in Reznikoff's poetry. He also reads some of Reznikoff's work, including Just before the sun goes down. This is class 1 of 4.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: David Cope part 1

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: A literature class, "Basic Poetics," taught by Allen Ginsberg at The Naropa Institue April 3, 1980. Ginsberg begins by discussing the prosody of Ezra Pound's Pisan Cantos, reading #80 in full, then segues into the bulk of the lecture centered around the prosody of English poet Ben Jonson. This is class 20 of 33.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg Basic Poetics, Class 20

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: A class in an Allen Ginsberg course on expansive poetics. The class opens with Ginsberg talking about the painter/poet Marsden Hartley. Ginsberg reads Hartley's I admire my native city, Spring, Drama number one, and Window cleaner to nude mannequin. The class does a choral reading of Vachel Lindsay's The Congo and talks about Lindsay's life. Ginsberg reads William Carlos Williams' To Elsie and a section of The Clouds. He ends the class by talking about Jaime de Angulo, and reads a portion of Bartolomeo Vanzetti's trial speech written by Angulo, called The trial. The class also discusses meter, rhythm and free verse.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg Class part 4 August 1981

docs.creator: Holman, Bob
docs.description: Second half of a Bob Holman 1991 Summer Writing Program class on music, poetry, rap and spoken word. Holman is briefly interviewed by a class member, on his life and involvement with poetry. He talks about the St. Mark's Poetry Project, Nuyorican Poets Cafe, his work with Anne Waldman, and his arrival at Naropa.(Continued from 91P134)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Bob Holman class, From rap to zap, July, 1991.

docs.creator: Holman, Bob
docs.description: First half of a Bob Holman 1991 Summer Writing Program class on music, poetry, rap and spoken word. Holman discusses a diversity of artists, including Was Not Was, Henry Rollins and deaf poet Peter Cook. He also addresses the problems of packaging and marketing poetry in a multimedia world. Holman shows the class a video of his production "Words in your face," featuring various poets, musicians and spoken word artists in performance. (Continues on 91P133)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Bob Holman class, From rap to zap, July, 1991.

docs.creator: Burroughs, William S.
docs.description: A William S. Burroughs reading compiled from a number of works. Burroughs covers topics from miracles and magic to the Titanic, narcotics, the supernatural and hospitals.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: William Burroughs reading, Art now: A day of contemporary art, July, 1989.

docs.creator: Pate, Alexs; Torres, Edwin
docs.description: First half of a reading with Alexis Pate and Edwin Torres. Pate reads from Multi-Culti. Torres reads and performs several pieces, including "Motor priest" and "Tempest." (Continues on 03P091)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Alexis Pate and Edwin Torres reading, July, 2003

docs.creator: Hollo, Anselm
docs.description: The third and final lecture in a series by Anselm Hollo, discussing the stakes of poetics within or outside accepted verse culture and by extension, accepted culture and politics in general. Hollo discusses the New York School, the Beats, the Black Mountain School, and the future of 21st century poetics. (Part 1 is on 01P001 and Part 2 is on 01P009.)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Anselm Hollo lecture, Letters to the new century, part 3, April, 2001.

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: A continuation of a Basic Poetics Class taught by Allen Ginsbergin 1980 at Naropa. In this class Ginsberg covers William Shakespeare's Sonnets. Topics include reading the sonnets as a novel of a love triangle between Shakespear, a young man, and the Dark Lady. Some works discussed and read include Sonnets 20 (the key to the sonnets), 18, 29, 33, 57 (the S and M sonnet), 64, 65, 73, 94, 116, 129, 144, 147, 152, and 153. This is class 16 of 33.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg Basic Poetics, Class 16

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: A class about the history of poetry, in a series of classes by Allen Ginsberg in 1975. Ginsberg discusses the work of Ezra Pound, 18th and 19th century poetics, and sound and rhythm in poetry. Ginsberg reads poetry selections, followed by a class discussion. (Continues on 75P008)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Allen Ginsberg class, The history of poetry, June 1975.

docs.creator: Moore, LeRoy
docs.description: This is tape 2 of a LeRoy Moore lecture on the history and theory of nonviolence. Moore talks about a few examples of nonviolent figures in history including Ghandi and MLK Jr. He describes Ghandi's theory on the three reactions to violence, Johann Galtung's personal and structural violence with examples of violent social structures and how modern structure fits into this. Moore also notes feminist influences on the theory of non-violence and the connection between property owning and violent action. The recording ends with Moore answering audience questions.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: LeRoy Moore class part 2 June 1986

docs.creator: Bateson, Gregory
docs.description: 71U031 is part 2 of Gregory Bateson's 1971 lecture on consciousness and psychopathology.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Gregory Bateson lecture on consciousness and psychopathology part 2 1971

docs.creator: Corso, Gregory
docs.description: Class instructed by Gregory Corso. The class covers various topics including the Zodiac cycle of history, poetry of the Aryan Age, Neanderthal magic, Sappho, Hermes, Gilgamesh, whales, fate, and Gnostics. This is class 1 of 8.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Gregory Corso class 1 July 1981

docs.creator: Corso, Gregory
docs.description: Class instructed by Gregory Corso. The class covers various topics including Shelley's birthday and biography, women poets, men as mystical/women as magical, and student poems. This is class 4 of 8.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Gregory Corso class 4 July 1981

docs.creator: Brown, Lee Ann; Jarnot, Lisa; Mayer, Bernadette
docs.description: Second half of a reading with Lisa Jarnot, Lee Ann Brown and Bernadette Mayer. This is a short conclusion with Mayer reading "Mind of hour" followed by a class collaboration. (Continued from 99P014)
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Lisa Jarnot, Lee Ann Brown and Bernadette Mayer reading, June, 1999.

docs.creator: Kyger, Joanne
docs.description: A class discussion led by Joanne Kyger on Gertrude Stein, July 1991. The biography of Stein from birth until death is based on a book by John Malcolm Brinnin called "The Third Rose: Gertrude Stein and Her Work." Biography includes major works and inspirations as well as personal anecdotes about Stein's life.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Joanne Kyger lecture on Gertrude Stein July 1991

docs.creator: Corso, Gregory
docs.description: Class instructed by Gregory Corso on poetry. Class begins with discussion on Thoreau and continues with student poems. The class concludes with an analysis of William Blake's Sick Rose. The tape ends with a piece of a separate class including Corso and Allen Ginsberg reading a poem. This is workshop 2 of 2.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Gregory Corso workshop 2 July 1981

docs.creator: Kyger, Joanne
docs.description: Part one of a class traught by Joanne Kyger in July 1977. In this class Joanne reads from her South Sea journals. She makes additional personal notes on the journals and the class discusses what she has read. This is the 4th class in a series.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Joanne Kyger Class Visiting Poets class 4 July 1977

docs.creator: Corso, Gregory; Kyger, Joanne
docs.description: This section of Beat and other Rebel Angels course taugh by Joanne Kyger in 1991 begins with students reading papers based on their learnings of Lew Welch. Joanne then proceeds to give a detailed account of Gregory Corso's life with anecdotal stories interspersed. She talks of his incarceration and first finding literature and writing while in Clinton jail and how he first met Allen Ginsberg. The students then read Corso's poem "Marriage." A tape of Corso reading his poems "All Survived," "High," and "The day after humankind" is also played. And in summation of this tape, Joanne reads Corso's "I gave way" and "The wholeness." Related tapes 91P183-91P195.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Joanne Kyger beat rebel angels class 6 November 1991

docs.creator: Joris, Pierre

docs.creator: Yau, John
docs.description: A lecture delivered by John Yau, June 27, 2002 for the Summer Writing Program at Naropa. Yau's lecture could be titled, How to Look at Art since 1945. In it he explores first Marcel Duchamp and the way in which contemporary art sprouted from his work in two directions: Hermetic and Legible and by extention explores Jasper Johns and Andy Warhol. Then back to Pollack and Wallace Berman, then from there, Yau extends further and brings us into a discussion of contemporary artists such as David Reed, Linda Besemen, Nancy Haynes, Catherine Grosse, and Pat Steir. This lecture was originaly presented with slides.

docs.creator: Blaser, Robin
docs.description: Robin Blaser presents another of his famously unsummarizable lectures, in which he searches with us for guides on the journey "From there to here to where: writing." "There" is Blaser's early childhood in Idaho, living in a train car and learning about syphilis from a tent chautauqua. "Here" is the hell that, as Pound said, holding his hands across his heart, is "here." "Where" is the question of where we are now, and where we are going, "eyes filled and deserted by the divine" (Jean-Luc Nancy). Along the way, Blaser makes use of guides that include Dante's "vernacular heart" and the contemporary poet's "vernacular task," and Giorgio Agamben and Jean-Luc Nancy's community after identity, discussing the writer's task as a Purgatory of debt and necessary transformation in which the irreparable separation from the divine gives rise to love.
docs.publisher: Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics
docs.title: Lecture with Robin Blaser June 2003

docs.description: This is the first day of a Leslie Scalapino workshop (7-17-1989) on the poetic diary form. She reads excerpts from her book "Way" and "That they were at te Beach." docs.description: Gregory Bateson lectures on "Orders of Change". docs.description: A class on Robert Creeley taught by Warren Tallman in 1991 at Naropa. Tallman's role in the San Francisco Renaissance put him in contact with many authors that shaped the later 20th century, including Charles Olson and Allen Ginsberg, which gives him a unique perspective on the poetry and life of Robert Creeley. docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: Second half of an Allen Ginsberg survey class on historical poetics. Ginsberg discusses topics, styles, and modes that he found useful in his own poetry, and that every poet should know. He includes a discussion of preliterate traditions; quantitative verse, including classic meters and long and short vowels; sonnets; song forms; and a discussion of poetry expressing states of consciousness. He shows how older forms are still alive in the work of contemporary poets, using as examples the works of Pound, Melville, Blake, Auden, Kerouac, Poe, Bob Dylan, and others. (Continued from 92P055)

docs.creator: Ginsberg, Allen
docs.description: This is the second portion of a class on Autobiographical Poetry/Writing. The class begins with Allen Ginsberg (AG) talking about the upcoming protest at Rocky Flats and there is much discussion about logistics. The class then reads from Reznikoff's Volume I and students begin sharing their material. Intermitently during the student readins, Allen provides feedback and gives concrete examples from their respective works on how to condense and improve the immediacy of the writing. Allen then references Joe Brainard's "I remember" and concludes the class by reading his own piece "White Shroud" which gets cut off by the end of the tape.

The first tape containing the readings of Anselm Hollo from two of his longer pieces entitled - Rue Willson Monday - and - Where, if Not Here - and Jerome Rothenberg who reads a number of his pieces which are all in three parts, beginning with the piece entitled - A Paradise of Poets.

docs.creator: Brownstein, Michael
docs.description: Michael Brownstein class on nineteenth century poetics focusing on Baudelaire. Brownstein finishes by reading Baudelaire's "Albatros," correspondences and the "Spleen" poems.

docs.title: Michael Brownstein class on nineteenth century poetics, Baudelaire and history, December, 1981.
